What does an ASR model do? 
Automatic speech recognition: speech in, text out. GLM - ASR - Nano does it in three steps.

The real recording: waveform, then spectrogram   Encoder output (illustration)   The 13 tokens it writes for the recording 
1. Hear 
The recording is about 56,000 
numbers: 3.5 s at 16 kHz. On the CPU 
it becomes a mel spectrogram: a 
picture of which pitches are loud at 
each moment. 
2. Listen 
The audio encoder reads the whole 
spectrogram and describes every 20 
ms of sound with 1280 numbers, using 
the sounds around it as context. 
3. Write 
The text decoder, a language model, 
writes the transcript one token at a 
time. A token is a word or a piece of 
one; the last one means “end”. 
Steps 2 and 3 run on the GPU. Their arithmetic is what your kernels compute.   02

What is a mel spectrogram? 
A picture of the sound: which pitches are loud at each moment. The model reads it like an image. 
sound 
high 
pitch 
↑ 
low 
0 s   1 s   2 s   3 s time → 
one column, zoomed in 
bar = loudness 
Like a music equalizer 
One column is a 10 ms 
snapshot: how loud each of 128 
pitch bands is, low at the 
bottom, high at the top. 100 
snapshots a second, side by 
side, make the picture. 
How to read it 
Time runs left to right, pitch bottom to 
top, and darker means louder. Vowels 
make dark stripes low down; “s” and “t” 
make smears high up. 
Why “mel” 
Ears tell low pitches apart far better 
than high ones: 100 vs 200 Hz is 
obvious, 7100 vs 7200 Hz is not. So 
the bands are narrow low down and 
wide high up. 
How it is made 
Cut the sound into 25 ms slices, one 
every 10 ms. Measure each pitch in 
every slice (a Fourier transform), add 
them up into 128 bands, take the log. 
Every recording is padded to 30 s, so the model always gets 128   ×   3000 numbers; this one fills the first 350 columns.   03

Each run keeps only the most likely

No KV cache 
Each run recomputes every position

The prompt is 59 positions: 15 tokens of instruction (“Please transcribe this audio into text”) and 44 of audio.   05

Inside one layer: where your kernels run 
Every encoder and decoder layer has this shape. The linear layers (Task 3) do almost all the arithmetic.

Step   Purpose   Task 
Norm   Keep the numbers at a steady scale, so dozens of stacked layers stay stable   Task 2 
q, k, v   Give each position a question (q), a label (k) and a message (v) for attention   Task 3 
RoPE   Tell attention where each position is, so that order matters   Task 1 
Attention   Let each position gather information from all the others: this is where context comes in   Task 4 
Out linear   Bring the gathered information back to the layer's width, then add the input back   Task 3 
MLP   Process each position on its own; about two thirds of the parameters are here   Task 3 
Calls per transcription: 2757 linear, 396 attention, 396 RoPE, 806 norm, 13 softmax.   06

Fill in the blanks 
Each blank is 1 to 15 lines. The code around them, the Python side and the tests are written for you. 
Do the tasks in order: each builds on the last, and Task 4 calls your Task 2 warp reductions.   07

How to do it 
One GPU per person:   only   -- gres=gpu:1, one GPU shell or job at a time. Exit when you are done. 
1. Get the code, set up once 
Clone   github.com/ed - aisys/edin - mls - 26 - autumn   on the head 
node, then run setup_env.sh. 
2. Get one GPU 
The head node has no GPU. Each session, ask Slurm for 
one card, put nvcc on PATH and activate mls - asr. 
3. Read the task guide 
docs/taskN - *.md: what the kernel computes, which thread 
does what, and what each blank needs. 
4. Fill in the blanks 
Replace // YOUR CODE HERE, then run make and fix every 
compiler error. 
5. Test, then run the model 
make testN compares your kernel with a CPU version. When 
it says ALL PASS, run the model with your kernels so far. 
# once,   on the head node (mlp) 
git clone   \ 
https://github.com/ed - aisys/edin - mls - 26 - autumn.git 
cd edin - mls - 26 - autumn/hw1 - asr 
bash setup_env.sh 
# every   session: ONE GPU (gpu:1) 
srun   - p Teaching   -- gres=gpu:1   \ 
-- cpus - per - task=2   -- mem=16G   \ 
-- time=01:00:00   -- pty bash 
export PATH=/opt/cuda - 12.8.0/bin:$PATH 
conda activate mls - asr 
cd ~/edin - mls - 26 - autumn/hw1 - asr 
# every   task, e.g. task   2 
make &&   make test2 
./run.sh   -- cuda task1,task2 
# all four done: the benchmark 
./run.sh   -- profile

The baseline: the same model on PyTorch 
What it is 
./run.sh   -- cuda none runs every operation with PyTorch instead of 
your kernels. Its matrix multiplies use cuBLAS, NVIDIA's tuned 
library. 
Why you run it 
First, to check your setup before you change any code. Then, as the 
reference your kernels are compared with. 
How to read it 
Time: mean   ±   std of 3 runs after 1 warm - up. Per token: the time 
divided by the 13 tokens. Accuracy: share of the expected words 
found; PASS above 80%.

02

The common pipeline 
Stage   Main operation   Output 
1 ASR interface   Transcribe the audio query   Transcript 
2 Local encoder   Encode the transcript with   enc_a   Query vector 
3 Exact retrieval   Rank corpus vectors by similarity   Top - k record IDs 
4 Context builder   Fetch text and construct the prompt   Evidence + question 
5 ELM generator   Generate an answer from the prompt   Answer + timings

Embeddings and exact retrieval 
Corpus matrix   24,000 records   ×   384 dimensions 
Similarity   Normalised query and corpus vectors use a dot product. 
ID mapping   Each vector row maps to a corpus record ID. 
enc_a   and   enc_b   Matching dimensions do not imply matching vector spaces.

Retrieval quality measures 
Measure   What it captures 
Recall@k   Fraction of relevant records found in the first k results 
MRR@10   Rank of the first relevant result, within the cutoff 
NDCG@10   Ranking quality with relevance gains and rank discount 
Toy example:   Two relevant records, one in top five: Recall@5 = 0.5 
Retrieval quality and final answer quality measure different stages. 
13

Answer evaluation   –   an evaluation aid 
Dimension   Scale   Focus 
Correctness   0 – 4   Factual and logical accuracy 
Grounding   0 – 4   Support from relevant evidence 
Completeness   0 – 4   Coverage of the answerable question 
Combined score   0 – 1   Sum of the three scores divided by 12 
Public judging uses the ASR transcript. It cannot verify that ASR preserved the intended question. 
Use this as an evaluation aid only, since this is purely generated by LLM. 
14

A fair systems experiment 
Comparison   State the baseline, intervention and expected trade - off. 
Controls   Keep inputs and unrelated model settings consistent. 
Measurements   Measure quality and the cost relevant to your question. 
Reproducibility   Describe timing boundaries, hardware, repeats and caches. 
How to find a good extension problem? 
15

Example of extension: retrieval depth 
Design choice   Experiment plan 
Variable   k = 2, 5, 10, 20 (baseline k = 5) 
Controls   Same transcripts, encoder, corpus and generator settings 
Quality   Recall@k   and answer correctness / grounding / completeness 
Cost   Context size and generation latency 
Analysis   When does extra evidence help, and when does it add noise? 
16

Other directions for investigation 
Direction   Possible question 
Batching   How does batch size affect throughput and query latency? 
Context selection   Can an evidence budget preserve quality with smaller prompts? 
Reranking   Does better evidence justify the additional stage cost? 
Dynamic updates   What is the cost of keeping the retrieval index consistent? 
Representation migration   How can a system transition between compatible representations? 
17 
You can also choose ASR optimisations as extensions.

The report’s chain of reasoning 
Part of the argument   What the reader needs 
Question   A precise problem and a reason it matters 
Method   Baseline, technical change and comparison controls 
Evidence   Quality and cost results that address the question 
Interpretation   Why the behaviour occurs and which trade - off it reveals 
Limitations   Conditions where the conclusion may not hold
